title: From flip flops to fisherman's sandals: Are your summer sandals killing your feet?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterFlip-flops have always been a popular solution to sweaty, uncomfortable feet in scorching wea
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterFlip-flops have always been a popular solution to sweaty, uncomfortable feet in scorching weather  - and now they've had a revamp. The most stylish way to wear them this summer is with a kitten heel, according to fashion expert and trend forecaster Angela Baidoo."It's not a high heel and it's really kind of easy to just slip in and slip out of," she says.However, heel or not, the flip-flop has earned itself a bad rap for lack of support and damaging our feet. Is that fair? Why your summer shoe could be bad for you"In terms of arch support and joint support, it's not the best style, but people are investing a bit more, getting their flip-flops customised, because it's something that is just so easy to wear," Baidoo says.Podiatrist Dr Helen Branthwaite, who is also chief clinical adviser at the Royal College of Podiatry, says it's "not accurate" to say flip-flops are bad.The problem comes if you go straight from wearing a very structured shoe to wearing flip-flops a lot, she explains. It means your foot is under more strain than normal, which makes you more prone to injury."The foot does start to change shape and tends to splay a little bit over time," says Branthwaite."A good analogy is if you were to wear a corset all the time and then took the corset off, everything would sort of all hang out, so to speak."So what are the stylish and comfortable alternatives?How to find healthy sandalsBaidoo suggests a more supportive flip-flop, such as a FitFlop, which is sturdier and contoured - a world away from the flat and thin flip-flops that have been cut from a big sheet of foam.Sliders are out and Crocs are in for Gen Z, she says. They might be "anti-fashion shoes" but they're "really comfy" and designed "orthopaedically" with footbed sandals like Birkenstocks offering the same advantages.The wooden clog is also making a comeback. It's worn by doctors and chefs on their feet all day. Scholl slider mules are the original orthopaedic shoe, Baidoo says - and admits she once had a pair in pink suede.Wedges are another option in the heat. "When I speak to some of my friends and some of my clients who work in the plus-size category, the wedge actually provides a form of comfortable footwear. And it provides a nice kind of silhouette for the ankle. You've got the support all the way through the shoe."Image source, Getty ImagesYou could always opt for the fisherman-style sandal, which looks like something a history teacher might have worn in the 1970s. With socks."Men can wear it as an alternative to a loafer. It's not as casual as a flip-flop, which might not be suitable for certain environments. It's a really cool kind of style to adopt for women too," Baidoo says.So what about the trend for wearing minimalist barefoot shoes? It's all about easing into them, says Branthwaite. In other words, don't buy a pair and then decide to go on a 5-mile hike.Expert tips for happy feet Podiatrist Dr Helen Branthwaite's top tips for looking after your feet: Pay close attention to the sole of the shoe and what it's made from, because that will influence how your foot moves and how you walkIf you can bend your flip-flops in two, then ask yourself if you're strong enough to take on the extra load your normal shoe would supportDon't forget to check the condition of your feet - the skin can dry out quickly in open footwear like flip-flops. You might not notice until your heel gets firmer and your toenails start to look fragileLather your feet in emollient, a moisturising water retention cream containing urea to hydrate the skin, every dayYour feet change constantly throughout your life, so get them measured regularly. Just because you start out being a size 6, doesn't mean you'll remain a size 6.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: From flip flops to fisherman's sandals: Are your summer sandals killing your feet?

title: Perez Hilton recovering in hospital after self-harming during TikTok livestream
description: US blogger Perez Hilton is recovering in hospital after members of the public reported that he had appeared to self-harm during a TikTok livestream.Em
body: US blogger Perez Hilton is recovering in hospital after members of the public reported that he had appeared to self-harm during a TikTok livestream.Emergency services were called to his home in Miami on Tuesday after concerned viewers reported a man "livestreaming acts of self-harm on social media".The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office told US media that an individual had been "safely recovered" and taken to "a local hospital, where he is receiving medical attention".Police added that their crisis response unit and licensed mental health professionals were also "on scene providing support and resources to the individual's family".If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.Hilton, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, was home alone during the time of the live stream, police confirmed, and had his TikTok account suspended soon after.In a statement issued to outlets including the LA Times, Newsweek and Rolling Stone, the Miami sheriff's office did not name Hilton but confirmed they had attended to reports of a man harming himself.After speaking with family members at the scene, deputies decided to "tactically disengage while continuing to monitor the situation", police said. "In many incidents involving a person experiencing a mental health crisis or actively harming themselves, deputies prioritise de-escalation by creating time, distance and opportunities for communication," their statement said."Unless there is an immediate threat to others, slowing the situation and utilizing crisis intervention techniques can reduce the likelihood of a suicide-by-cop encounter and minimise the risk of injury to the individual, deputies and the public."Suicide by cop is a US term for when individuals try to end their lives by behaving in a way that will provoke police into killing them.In a later update, the Sheriff's Office said the man had been transported to a hospital, adding that mental health professionals were at the scene "providing support and resources to the individual's family".BBC News has asked representatives for Hilton for comment, and also contacted TikTok and Miami police. The celebrity blogger's managers, Dante Rusciolelli and Rebekah Kochan, told outlets including Variety, external in a joint statement that they were "aware of the concerning content circulating online involving our client, Perez Hilton."At this time, we have not been able to make direct contact with him, despite our ongoing efforts to reach him," they continued. "Our primary concern is Perez's health and well-being, as well as the well-being of his family."Until we have confirmed information, we will not speculate or comment further. We appreciate everyone's concern and ask that his privacy be respected during this time."Hilton rose to fame in the early 2000s via his popular and at-times controversial celebrity gossip website.Perez Hilton was a stage name he chose as a play on Paris Hilton, who was one of the most written about celebrities at the time.His often snarky takes have drawn criticism over the years from some celebrities, including Miley Cyrus, Khloe Kardashian, Mila Kunis and his former friend Lady Gaga.But in recent years, Hilton apologised for cruel comments made in his early career and made efforts to change his online brand, reflecting a wider change in online culture and the way celebrity news is covered.He adopted a kinder, more family-friendly public persona while also embracing fatherhood - he has three children via surrogacy."I have a ton of regrets, particularly because I now see that I never needed to be so mean or cruel," he wrote in his 2020 memoir."One of the many things I regret is that I hurt so many people by giving them nasty nicknames, and above all that I was unkind to the children of celebrities."Hilton continues to cover showbiz news via his online blog, social media platforms and weekly podcast.

schema.headline: Perez Hilton recovering in hospital after self-harming during TikTok livestream

title: Anthropic AI created fake profiles and impersonated people in attempted hack
description: Two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in an attempted cyber-attack during testing by the UK's
body: Two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in an attempted cyber-attack during testing by the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).In the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people.AISI said on Tuesday Mythos - and OpenAI's Sol - AI models had engaged in a level of "autonomy and deception" it had not seen before, though it clarified most of the malicious actions were carried out by Mythos.Anthropic and OpenAI noted in response to AISI's report that its test had reduced or removed normal safeguards.AISI evaluators first noticed "unusual data transfers leaving our research systems" during a test, then found that "some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations".In the most serious case, a Mythos agent followed the routine of a human cyber-attacker by trying to trick people into giving it access to GitHub, a large platform where technology developers store software code.The agent was trying to insert "malicious code" into GitHub's system.It identified and researched the people who maintained GitHub and created a series of fake accounts based on those real people. It sent messages and files through a file-sharing service as part of an effort to pressure and trick the people into approving its malicious code.When challenged, "it edited its earlier activity to appear harmless and considered adopting a fresh identity to continue," AISI said.Throughout the attempts, it was human review that stopped the agent from succeeding in delivering the malicious code to GitHub.While AISI said the Mythos agent had not been instructed specifically to avoid or carry out such behaviour, it was "the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world".The rival AI companies, which are poised to be listed on the public stock market, have been in the headlines in recent weeks after announcing their tools were responsible for several cyber-hacking incidents.  Anthropic wrote in a public statement that the AISI testing parameters were "not representative of any of our production models".It added that the company is conducting its own investigation into the incident in order to "identify the causes of its behavior".A spokesperson for OpenAI said the AISI testing conditions "do not reflect ordinary use" and that the company would "continue working with evaluators and other stakeholders across the industry to strengthen shared practices for conducting evaluations safely as models become more capable".AISI said on Tuesday its testing of AI models in this way was routine, though it acknowledged these were "conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public".But it said giving AI access to the open internet gave "a more realistic sense of what a model may be capable of" in the hands of nefarious hackers.It added that the model behaviour at issue amounted to "a small number of events under very specific conditions".Nonetheless, it said the way Mythos and Sol acted in response to a straightforward task went outside of what the AI tools were prompted to do."The activity undertaken by the agent showed signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate", AISI said.AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said identifying and sharing these types of risks "is exactly what AISI was set up to do". He added it was important to understand AI to "make it safer to use and ensure people can go on to benefit from it in their lives and at work".The relevant tests started on 25 July and were spotted by AISI on 28 July.The Insitutue had asked each of the models to "solve a cybersecurity challenge" that involved GitHub, the software code repository, which is owned by Microsoft.GitHub and the affected users were notified by AISI of the attempted breaches.GitHub told the BBC it had disabled the fake accounts in accordance with its policies. Additional reporting by Chris Vallance

schema.headline: Anthropic AI created fake profiles and impersonated people in attempted hack

title: Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv kills at least 17
description: Russia has attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and drones, killing at least 17 people, as Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said interceptor
body: Russia has attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and drones, killing at least 17 people, as Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said interceptors "could have saved lives".In one of the deadliest strikes on Kyiv and the capital region this year - which started after midnight on Wednesday - at least 45 people were injured after residential buildings, a railway station and warehouses were hit.Ukraine, who has consistently urged allies for more US-made Patriot missile interceptors to defend against Russian ballistics, has not reported intercepting any of the missiles in the overnight attack.Zelensky added delays in receiving anti-ballistic systems from partners leads to "horrific casualties and destruction".The Russia defence ministry said it had struck logistics hubs and supply centres in Kyiv and the surrounding region."These centres were involved in the storage, delivery of various weapons and military supplies, as well as in the production and distribution of unmanned aerial vehicles," it said.It also said it had hit three cargo vessels "which were transporting weapons and military equipment" near the Black Sea port of Odesa.Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said there were fears people could be trapped under rubble.Ukraine's emergency services said one person had died in the city of Kyiv and at least 16 injured, with a further 16 dead and 29 injured in the wider region.Fires were still being extinguished in five locations across the region on Wednesday, covering an area of approximately 230,000 sq m, it added.The country's air force said in a post on Telegram that Russia had launched 24 ballistic missiles and four anti-ship missiles during the attack on the capital.The air force added that 115 drones had been launched by Russia during the attack and air defence systems intercepted 98 of them.Russia has intensified attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, while Ukraine has also increased its attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure, including power facilities.Dmitry Milyaev, the governor of Russia's Tula region, said on Wednesday that a drone had crashed into a warehouse of e-commerce giant Wildberries in the region overnight and caused a fire.He said on Telegram that one person had been injured and there had been no deaths reported, with the retailer saying firefighting teams were working at the site and the facility had been evacuated pre-emptively.Ukraine has repeatedly targeted warehouses, including those operated by Wildberries. Five people were killed and 10 wounded in the Moscow region on Tuesday morning in the most recent strikes on warehouses.The day before, Russian officials said seven people were killed and 58 injured after a drone hit a busy beach in the southern Krasnodar region.Ukraine, meanwhile, expressed outrage over a video showing a man chased by a drone in Kherson, calling it a deliberate "hunt" and "safari" targeting civilians.Both sides have denied deliberately targeting civilians.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday the EU had received €1.4bn (£1.2bn) from immobilised Russian assets, which would be used to support Ukraine in its war against Russia.

schema.headline: Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv kills at least 17

title: Police chief considers legal action over PC Harper killers' early release
description: The chief constable of Thames Valley Police says he will consider joining legal action to block the release of two of PC Andrew Harper's killers.Chief
body: The chief constable of Thames Valley Police says he will consider joining legal action to block the release of two of PC Andrew Harper's killers.Chief Constable Jason Hogg told the BBC he was in discussion with the Police Federation of England and Wales over the matter, adding public opinion on their potential release was "overwhelming".PC Harper, who served with Thames Valley, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire. The two passengers in the car, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, were sentenced in 2020 to 13 years for manslaughter and could apply for early release after serving half of their sentences.The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and is not eligible for early release. Speaking on the Today programme, Thames Valley Police chief Jason Hogg urged the government to reconsider its position.Only prisoners convicted of murder, rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from the scheme in England and Wales - while those convicted of manslaughter remain eligible."I fully understand the challenges around the crisis in the prison system," he said. "But the decision made and where that line has been drawn, I do not believe that people responsible for taking the life of another citizen in our country should be released early." He said on Wednesday: "I was informed yesterday that the Police Federation are considering legal action, I am in discussions with the Police Federation with regards to this matter".Asked whether this meant he would join them, he said: "I think we need to get some legal advice in relation to this. This is something I certainly would consider."After campaigning by PC Harper's wife Lissie following his death, Parliament passed "Harper's Law", which gives mandatory life sentences to the killers of emergency services workers. It doubles the maximum penalty from 12 months to two years for those who assault police or other emergency workers. But the new rules - introduced in 2022 - did not apply in the sentencing of the police officer's killers, and so do not prevent them from being released early. Hogg said: "The law isn't retrospective and we all understand that, but the fact that they are released early simply seems perverse."Aileen O'Connor, branch chair of Thames Valley Police Federation also told the BBC her organisation was considering legal action."We are in talks this morning, I'll get an update this afternoon whether that is an avenue that we can explore and if it is an avenue we can explore then I'll get behind that 110%," she told BBC Breakfast.As for what shape a potential legal challenge might take, she said: "Ultimately that's for the specialists, the barristers and those in that legal sector to make that decision whether there is a challenge there."If there is a challenge then we will look to take that challenge."Sentencing Minister Jake Richards told the BBC it would be wrong to pick out individual cases and block two of PC Harper's killers from early release.Although the government had reviewed what sentences would be excluded from the early release scheme, he confirmed "manslaughter is not one of those offences". Richards said: "It would be wrong to pick out individual cases within different offending cohorts. That wouldn't be right. It wouldn't be lawful either. So it is correct that those two individuals will be subject to the new regime from October".On Tuesday Justice Secretary Alex Norris warned a prison capacity crisis would be likely if fewer prisoners were allowed early release.Norris apologised to families who would be affected by the early release scheme and stressed that the government wanted to go further "but we cannot". "We have to make this decision, we've been able to make some changes to it, but we have to have the rest of the sentencing act changes otherwise we run out of prison places in November and that can't happen," he said.The justice secretary said 5,000 extra releases will take place in 10 batches from October.Approximately 1,000 prisoners will now not be released early following the revision to the scheme, he clarified.The government also announced an extra £10m will go to front-line victim support services, including a new national helpline.

schema.headline: Police chief considers legal action over PC Harper killers' early release

title: Trump says Iran will be 'hit very hard' if Hormuz Strait not open soon as oil prices fall
description: Donald Trump said the Strait of Hormuz would open "very soon" or Iran would be "hit very hard" as oil prices fell to a three-week low amid hopes of a
body: Donald Trump said the Strait of Hormuz would open "very soon" or Iran would be "hit very hard" as oil prices fell to a three-week low amid hopes of a deal.The US president was speaking to Fox News after Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent both said talks had progressed to allow shipments potentially to resume later this week.On Tuesday, the cost of a barrel of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, fell by almost 5% to under $80 (£60) on the news of supply disruptions potentially being eased. It continued to move lower on Wednesday - down about 0.7% in Asian trading.But the failure of previous talks in recent months to de-escalate the conflict has led to a volatile oil market, with motorists ultimately being hit by higher fuel prices."We're having very good discussions," Trump said during a visit to California, insisting Iran was keen to seal a deal to bring an end to months of conflict.US Central Command (CentCom) said the "southern route through the Strait of Hormuz remains free and open for all commercial vessels seeking to transit the international waterway".On Tuesday, along with the drop in Brent crude, US West Texas Intermediate prices were down more than 5%, to $76 a barrel. Both contracts dropped to their lowest levels since 13 July.Rubio said there had been progress made in discussions on getting more ships through the strait with Iran and Oman."There's been progress made in those talks, but not finality yet. We're hoping that will happen very shortly," he told reporters at the State Department.Bessent said a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could be agreed as soon as Wednesday.There was a "chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalised position in this conflict," he told CNBC."It would be freedom of movement," he added, when asked whether Iran would be allowed to charge for ships passing through.While senior figures in the US government have announced talks have been progressing, no details of what a potential deal may look like have been released.Iran has said it is not negotiating with the US - and has no plans to do so - and is instead talking to Oman.A spokesman for Iran's foreign ministry said that talks with Oman, a mediator in negotiations, on a new mechanism for vessels going through the Strait, had been positive. Qatar, which is a key mediator between Washington and Tehran, said it was continuing efforts with other mediators to try to achieve a diplomatic resolution to the war, but admitted no direct talks were currently planned.With the conflict continuing to drag on, the US has used nearly all of its global stockpile of long-range precision missiles, two sources with direct knowledge of the matter told the BBC's US news partner CBS News.The Strait of Hormuz has been a central point in negotiations between the US and Iran. Before the conflict began in late February, the waterway handled about one-fifth of global daily oil and liquefied natural gas supplies.Iran has halted most traffic through the Strait since the conflict began, while the US has also imposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports in the region.Another blockade is in place on Saudi Arabia's ports in the Red Sea, imposed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since 20 July.The route had become a crucial alternative since Iran blocked the strait, but it has become increasingly dangerous, with a spate of attacks on vessels reported in the past week.On Tuesday, a projectile sank an Indian-flagged vessel near Yemeni waters, the India's shipping minister said, with all 14 on board rescued.Analysts believe the threat to ships carrying oil in the Middle East is at its worst since the Iran war started."Investors are acutely aware of how many times we've already been at this point in the war and how fragile the process of securing lasting agreements can be," said Danni Hewson, head of financial analysis at AJ Bell.The disruption has sent prices at the pumps up across the world. In the UK petrol prices are now at levels seen at the start of the conflict, with the average cost of a litre of petrol hitting £1.60, according to the RAC motoring group.In the US, gasoline prices are on average above $4 a gallon, according to the AAA. Diesel is almost $5.40 a gallon.Prices have surged to above $120 when the conflict has escalated and plunged in response to previous talks suggesting a breakthrough. The elevated prices have led to major oil companies, such as BP, Shell, Chevron and Exxon Mobil, to report bumper profits.However, Hewson added that despite the huge revenues, oil companies were "at the mercy" of US President Donald Trump's "machinations".On Monday, Trump warned Iran faced its "last chance" to agree a deal to allow commercial shipping to resume in the Strait.He said he had called off "massive" strikes on the country for talks to resume. US stock markets were trading higher on Tuesday following news of the negotiations lowering oil prices and also in response to corporate results related to Artificial Intelligence.Investors have experienced jitters on Wall Street as results from Big Tech firms indicate spending on the technology is set to continue to soar.

schema.headline: Trump says Iran will be 'hit very hard' if Hormuz Strait not open soon as oil prices fall

title: Afghan boxer arrives at Greek court in connection with death of Scottish woman
description: Figure caption, Sharif Ahmadzai leaving court after the hearingByBen PhilipReporting fromAthens and Megan BonarBBC ScotlandUpdated 1 hour agoThe man s
body: Figure caption, Sharif Ahmadzai leaving court after the hearingByBen PhilipReporting fromAthens and Megan BonarBBC ScotlandUpdated 1 hour agoThe man suspected of killing a Scottish aid worker in Greece has appeared in court in Athens.The body of Elisabeth Jane Ross was found in a suitcase at an abandoned building on 18 July, days after she had been reported missing.Sharif Ahmadzai, who is 26 and from Afghanistan, was told during the private court hearing that he faces charges of homicide with intent, robbery and weapons offences.He made no comment and the case was deferred until Thursday, when it is expected that Ahmadzai will be formally charged.Homicide with intent is equivalent to a murder charge in Scots law.Ahmadzai was driven to court in a grey Hyundai i30 with blacked out windows for the hearing.Image source, FacebookImage caption, Elisabeth Jane Ross is believed to have been working with immigrants in GreeceHe was escorted from the court more than an hour later by police officers with their faces covered. He kept his head down as he walked from the building back to the car.Police said Ross - who is from Edinburgh and is known to family and friends as Lisa - had been volunteering with a refugee support group based in Athens.She arrived in Greece on 26 June and stayed in the Kertasini area of Piraeus until 10 July.Her body was found in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July.Police said the coroner's initial report failed to determine a cause of death, but more detailed examinations concluded it was an "obvious criminal act, likely asphyxiation".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, arrived at the court building in a grey carThe BBC understands Ahmadzai, who left Afghanistan after being orphaned aged 15, lives in Greece with his American wife and their child.After leaving his home country, he travelled to Greece via Iran and Turkey, according to a video telling his story, external which was published by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).He then settled in a refugee camp on the island of Lesbos, where he met his wife and converted to Christianity.The couple then set up the charity Love Every Nation Athens to help other refugees.He won a Greek super lightweight boxing title earlier this year.The president of the Union of Police Officers of Southeast Attica, George Kalliakmanis, said it was "possible" Ross and Ahmadzai had crossed paths through charity work.He said they were investigating whether Ahmadzai had a key to the apartment Ross was staying in.The union said it had verified footage appearing to show Ahmadzai carrying a suitcase which is believed to have contained the body.It added that a location sharing app, used by Ahmadzai's wife, showed that the suspect had been at the property in Rethymnou Street where Ross is thought to have died.Kalliakmanis said Ahmadzai had admitted moving the body but denied murder, claiming he had found Ross dead in the bathroom.The officer said police believed the suspect took the victim's bank card and phone, and "made sure" to send text messages to her family and friends to "make it seem like she was still alive".He said the police also believed the suspect used the victim's bank card to make withdrawals totalling "around €10,000".Kalliakmanis added that Ahmadzai's wife had no involvement or prior knowledge of the alleged crime.Additional reporting by Daphne Toli in Athens

schema.headline: Afghan boxer arrives at Greek court in connection with death of Scottish woman

title: Undercover reporter offered fenbendazole and ivermectin as cancer treatment
description: Dewormer and scabies drugs being sold as cancer treatments, BBC investigation findsFigure caption, Stairlift salesman Jason Sarver supplied the BBC wi
body: Dewormer and scabies drugs being sold as cancer treatments, BBC investigation findsFigure caption, Stairlift salesman Jason Sarver supplied the BBC with fenbendazole and ivermectin tablets for £100ByPaul Heaney and Sian VivianBBC Wales InvestigatesUpdated 5 hours agoAnimal dewormer and a drug used to treat scabies are being sold and promoted as unproven cancer treatments, a BBC investigation has found.Following a tip off, an undercover journalist was able to buy fenbendazole and ivermectin from a stairlift salesman in south Wales, and also found them for sale on Amazon.Macmillan Cancer Support said it was concerned by the findings and that a growing number of people were asking about the medicines, despite "no clinical evidence" that they work.Amazon removed the products after we contacted them, and said it had "proactive measures in place" to stop prohibited products being listed by third-party sellers.Senior doctors are worried vulnerable patients could be put at risk by taking the medicines, as they say it could harm or delay conventional treatment.Six months ago, Rebecca Holder contacted the BBC after a visit from stairlift salesman Jason Sarver.She said Sarver and her father Bob, who had a brain tumour, lung cancer and needed help with his mobility, had been discussing stairlifts when the salesman changed the topic to talk about the drugs. Image source, Rebecca HolderImage caption, Bob (pictured) had been discussing stairlifts with a salesman when he started talking about the unproven cancer treatmentIvermectin is an anti-parasitic drug used to treat conditions like scabies, while fenbendazole is an animal dewormer. The BBC has seen videos and social posts with thousands - sometimes millions - of views, with unproven claims that these medicines could help treat cancer.Hollywood actor Mel Gibson claimed on a popular US podcast that the drugs successfully treated three of his friends who had cancer."Jason started to say that he could get hold of a treatment that wasn't available on the NHS, that was known to shrink brain tumours," Rebecca said. "So I wrote down everything he said about these medicines... fenbendazole, ivermectin... I couldn't quite believe what he was saying."Rebecca said Sarver offered to sell her dad, from Monmouthshire, the medicines.Undercover: Cancer Cure or Con?An undercover investigation looks at claims surrounding an unproven "cancer treatment"An undercover BBC reporter contacted Sarver posing as someone with a relative who had cancer.He repeated the same claims and sent a link to videos making unproven assertions that the drugs were effective against cancer."I do a lot of research, medical papers, white papers, anything that comes out fresh, I am on it," Sarver said. "I'm not a doctor, I just pass what I hear on."He went on to supply the BBC with fenbendazole and ivermectin tablets for £100 which he said would be "two to three months' supply" to treat lung cancer and "other cancers as well".He said his work selling stairlifts meant he saw "a lot of ill people"."I can't help myself, I've got to tell them about it," he said.Image caption, The BBC found fenbendazole and ivermectin on multiple websites offering delivery to UK addresses, and successfully made several orders with AmazonIvermectin is a prescription-only medicine in the UK, which means it can only be given by a licensed person, such as a doctor or pharmacist.It gained global attention as a potential "miracle drug" during the coronavirus pandemic, although clinical trials have consistently shown it does not provide clinical benefits for Covid-19 patients.The MHRA medical regulator said it was not licensed for cancer treatment.Animal dewormer fenbendazole is an anti-parasitic drug which is not licensed for use in humans in the UK.It can be bought in small quantities for animals without a prescription, according to the Veterinary Medicines Directorate.While some trials exist into their anti-cancer properties, Macmillan Cancer Support said there was "zero real-world clinical evidence" to back up the claims about ivermectin.The charity's chief medical officer, Prof Richard Simcock, said he was concerned the BBC was able to easily buy the medicines without a prescription."We're seeing an increasing number of people asking about these two products," he said."We're worried that they're not getting up-to-date, effective and accurate information about what these drugs are capable of. "If someone is thinking about taking these drugs, we'd really urged them to talk to their clinical team or ring the clinical helplines at Macmillan where we can provide information about what safe and effective care might look like."He added this kind of misinformation was often fuelled by the appeal of personal anecdotes, especially if they came from someone a person already knows.Cancer Research UK also warned that, while there was some anti-cancer data from testing fenbendazole using mice, there was no scientific evidence to prove that it worked in people.Image source, Jared WrightImage caption, Jared says his mother put her hope into the drugs instead of seeing an oncologist Jared Wright, from Wisconsin in the USA, told the BBC that his mother Kelly started taking ivermectin and fenbendazole after being diagnosed with cancer last year.He said she ignored doctors' advice to accept conventional treatment and became a "victim of misinformation about cancer", putting her faith in the drugs in the hope of a cure. "They were delivered to our house, these pill bottles, and she just started eating the ivermectin and the fenbendazole three times a day," Jared said. "All she had read online was that it cures cancer."Image source, Jared WrightImage caption, Kelly put her faith in ivermectin and fenbendazole in the hope of a cureJared said his mother died shortly after her 63rd birthday in January."It was a horrible death. She was shaking, she couldn't see, she had this glaze over her eyes, she couldn't speak anymore," he said. "She had another 20 years or more - she would be alive right now if she had the correct information, if she had listened to me and gone to an oncologist."The BBC discovered it was easy to get hold of the drugs that Kelly hoped would save her.We found multiple websites offering delivery to UK addresses and successfully made several orders with Amazon. Supplying prescription-only medicines is an offence under the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 unless you are an "appropriate practitioner" such as a doctor or a pharmacist. The MHRA said, where there was evidence that a veterinary medicine is supplied for humans or a prescription-only medicine is sold by someone other than a qualified healthcare professional, it could take enforcement action, including criminal investigation and prosecution.Since 2024, it has seized 27,500 doses of fenbendazole and 124,000 doses of ivermectin intended for human use, working in conjunction with Border Force. Image caption, Consultant oncologist Martin Rolles says unproven drugs could make cancer treatment toxic or less effectiveMartin Rolles, a consultant oncologist with 25 years of experience at the South West Wales Cancer Centre, warned the drugs could interact with proven cancer medication and either make treatment more toxic or less effective."There's also the risk that the drugs themselves could cause side effects and make the patient unwell, which might stop them being able to receive conventional cancer treatment," he said. He added the reason ivermectin was not part of conventional treatment was because there were "no good human trials... for use against cancer"."There's certainly some interesting laboratory data but that's not the same as clinical evidence," he said, adding there was also not enough data on fenbendazole as a cancer treatment, so "therefore it is unsafe".Image caption, Liz O'Riordan says she has seen people die after believing anecdotes about unproven cancer treatment Three-time cancer survivor and former surgeon Liz O'Riordan now uses YouTube to answer cancer questions and challenge conspiracy theories. She said she knew of people dying after believing anecdotes about unproven cancer treatment. "Anecdotes and testimonials are now the strongest forms of evidence - 'my aunt on Facebook did this, therefore it must be true'," she said. "You don't know their medical records, they could be having other treatment as well."I see the other side, I see the people where it doesn't work, where they got sick, where they died."She continued: "It's that fear of death - you want control, you want hope, you want to be that one person who's going to make it."I just worry it's getting bigger, and if we don't all take notice and start to do something about it, we're going to be in a very dark place in a couple of years' time."The BBC contacted Sarver to ask why he sold the drugs, but he declined to comment.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Undercover reporter offered fenbendazole and ivermectin as cancer treatment

title: How AI is changing jobs in the Philippines' outsourcing industry
description: 'I feel like I dug my own grave': The workers caught in the AI transitionImage source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, The Philippines is kno
body: 'I feel like I dug my own grave': The workers caught in the AI transitionImage source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, The Philippines is known as the call centre capital of the worldBySuranjana TewariAsia Business CorrespondentReporting fromManilaFor 15 years, single mother Lisa made a living from content writing.She began writing straight out of college, freelanced for years and eventually followed a path taken by many young Filipinos: joining a multinational in the country's booming outsourcing industry.Lisa says she never felt the need to use artificial intelligence (AI) in her work."I can say that I am able to do my job, I meet deadlines. In my opinion, there is no need for [AI]," she told the BBC. Eight months into her latest role, and one month before the position was due to become permanent, she was made redundant.In the months before, Lisa says a public relations agency had been tasked with producing AI-generated material that she and her colleagues were asked to edit. She says her skills were used to train the AI on the company writing style."I feel like I dug my own grave," she says. "We were the ones who trained the artificial intelligence that replaced us."Lisa, not her real name, is one of several former outsourcing employees the BBC spoke to who asked to remain anonymous. They signed confidentiality agreements in return for severance pay, and fear that speaking publicly could hurt their chances of finding work in an industry which has a small network.Their experiences offer an insight into a question confronting emerging economies like the Philippines: what happens when AI begins to automate the jobs that helped lift millions of people into the middle classes?Building an industryEvery evening around 5pm, streams of workers wearing company lanyards spill out of high-rise offices in the district of Cubao in Manila.It's one of several areas of the capital where multinational companies have premises – providing all sorts of outsourcing work including call centres, accounting, software development and marketing copy services for clients thousands of miles away.For over two decades, these business districts have symbolised one of the Philippines' biggest economic success stories.Beginning in the early 2000s, the country was promoted as an English-speaking alternative to India for what's called business process outsourcing (BPO).Successive governments offered tax incentives, invested in infrastructure and encouraged multinational companies to set up large operations.Global groups like Accenture, Concentrix and Teleperformance built sprawling campuses, employing hundreds of thousands of Filipinos.Today, the outsourcing industry employs roughly 1.9 million people, and generates $40bn (£30.1bn) in revenues every year, accounting for about 10% of the Philippines' economy.But experts say the industry is disproportionately vulnerable to the impact of AI.Image caption, The outsourcing industry employs about 1.9 million people in the PhilippinesThe International Labour Organization estimates that 12.7 million Filipinos - more than one in four workers - are employed in occupations exposed to generative AI, the highest share in South East Asia.The organisation expects many roles to change rather than disappear but the types of service jobs that people do in the Philippines leaves it particularly at risk.Jack Madrid, president of the IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines (IBPAP), admits that AI is being adopted by the sector. More than two-thirds of IBPAP's members are already running AI pilots, he says."Agentic AI has the potential to automate at a much more accelerated pace," Madrid says. "Obviously, there's a layer of jobs that are automatable or have been automated."But he adds that the vast majority of affected workers have been redeployed within the same organisations.Madrid says any weakness in hiring reflects more than the impact of AI."We've seen a slowdown in investment decisions on whether certain job functions or processes should be offshored," he says, pointing to slower global demand and uncertainty over how companies will ultimately deploy the technology.Even so, he acknowledges the challenge. "We cannot do enough to be prepared," he says. "The importance of reskilling" cannot be overstated.The pressure to automateMary, another former content writer whose name we've changed, says her employer encouraged the use of AI as a productivity tool.Instead of making her job easier, she says it created additional responsibilities."We had to edit more, fact-check more because the data AI produced was inaccurate," she says. "Technically it was more work for us."Like Lisa, she was later made redundant.Companies are under pressure to implement AI, to reduce costs and increase productivity, experts say. Teleperformance, the world's largest call centre operator and one of the Philippines' biggest private employers, has said AI offers an opportunity to augment rather than replace its workforce.The company expects AI to handle routine interactions while human agents move into more complex roles. Teleperformance has also said it plans to retrain employees.Accenture has similarly said that generative AI will reshape almost every job rather than eliminate positions.The firm has promised to invest billions of dollars in AI capabilities and workforce training.Concentrix - which is the biggest outsourcing firm in the Philippines - says its AI systems should remain under human oversight and has committed to training employees in the new technology.Some Filipino managers are uneasy about AI and want to slow down adoption, according to Paul Quintos, from the University of the Philippines-Diliman. They are concerned about how much of the domestic workforce might be displaced."But there's tremendous pressure from foreign clients to adopt AI," he says. "It's a major cost-cutting measure."Philippine outsourcing companies compete directly with rivals in India and elsewhere for contracts from multinational corporations.Increasingly, those clients expect suppliers not only to provide cheaper labour, but also to integrate AI into the services they deliver.Image caption, The BBC spoke to employees who say they trained AI before being let goDespite hundreds of billions of dollars being invested globally in AI, Quintos says there is still limited evidence about how much productivity many workplace tools actually deliver."There is a term called 'AI washing'," he says.Some layoffs are presented as being driven by AI when companies are in fact responding to weaker demand or slowing economic conditions, Quintos says.Attributing redundancies to AI, he adds, can make restructuring appear like technological progress rather than a response to market conditions.The next transitionLabour groups have told the BBC that existing employment laws in the Philippines govern redundancy but offer little guidance on how companies should introduce AI into workplaces or consult employees over its use.The Philippines' outsourcing sector is also non-unionised, leaving many workers with little formal say over how new technologies are deployed.The government says that it, and the private sector have a responsibility to retrain workers, and risks falling behind competitors like India and Singapore. "To be completely honest, I think we're slightly behind. We have to catch up," says Leandro Aguirre of the Philippines Department of Information and Communications Technology."We have to double our efforts to put our people in a position where they will not be displaced but actually thrive in this growing AI race."The government has committed to upskilling more than 300,000 outsourcing workers, but Aguirre acknowledges that the Philippines may need to rethink the economic model that helped make it an outsourcing centre."We relied heavily on foreign direct investment," he says. "But I think we also need to focus on local talent and local companies."The ambition, he says, is to build home-grown AI companies capable of creating higher-value jobs.Aguirre rejects calls for sweeping new AI legislation, arguing that existing labour, privacy and consumer protection laws can be adapted more quickly through regulatory guidance."The benefits of AI have to trickle down to people," he says. "It can't just benefit employers."For more than 20 years, the Philippines built one of the world's most successful outsourcing industries by selling the skills of its people to multinational companies.AI may not end that model, but it is certainly changing it, and risks leaving some workers behind.Additional reporting by Jaltson Akkanath Chummar and Regine Cabato

schema.headline: How AI is changing jobs in the Philippines' outsourcing industry

title: Marcus Rashford: Will he return to Man Utd - and what impact would he have?
description: What happens next with Rashford and Man Utd?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Marcus Rashford made six appearances for England at the World Cup
body: What happens next with Rashford and Man Utd?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Marcus Rashford made six appearances for England at the World CupByManchester United reporterThe unlikely Manchester United reunion is close to completion.When Marcus Rashford was unveiled by Barcelona in July 2025, at the start of a season-long loan, no-one expected he would find himself back at Old Trafford 12 months later.United gave his coveted number 10 shirt to new arrival Matheus Cunha.Rashford was also looking to the future as he assessed the move to Spain."[Manchester United] is in a period of change and have been for a while," the forward said at his Barca unveiling last summer."I don't have anything bad to say as it has been an important part, not just of my career but my life, so I was grateful for the opportunity. I wish them all the best and hope they are successful in the future."Barring an unexpected late twist, that future will now include him.If his return to United is in line with the club's other World Cup players, who have all come back about three weeks after their final game in the tournament, he will be involved in next week's Maynooth training camp in the Republic of Ireland.Should that happen, his first game could be against an AC Milan side managed by former boss Ruben Amorim, in Wroclaw on 15 August, depending on what his current manager, Michael Carrick, views as the wisdom of Rashford featuring against Leeds at Croke Park on 12 August with just a couple of days' training behind him.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Marcus Rashford jumps for joy after scoring for Barcelona against Real MadridAt virtually every stage of the past year, the expectation was Rashford would not spend the 2026-27 season at Manchester United.He scored 11 goals and made 14 assists as Barca won the La Liga title, the Spanish Super Cup and reached the Champions League quarter-finals.When Barcelona decided not to activate the £26m clause to buy the 28-year-old, whose United contract expires in 2028, it was thought to be a negotiating tactic, aimed at taking Rashford on another loan.But the signing of German winger Karim Adeyemi from Borussia Dortmund on 23 July, following the arrival of England winger Anthony Gordon, seemed to end that possibility.Rashford posted a farewell note to the club on social media on 30 July. A day later, Barca manager Hansi Flick was asked about the forward following a pre-season game at Birmingham."He is a fantastic player and a fantastic person," said Flick. "The team miss him, I will miss him, but it is life. This is what we have to accept."Can Rashford have a positive impact at Man Utd?That reality has created a new one.Rashford is contracted to Manchester United until 2028. His salary of £325,000 a week makes him the club's top earner at a time when minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe is trying to stay on top of wage costs, which is, by some distance, the club's highest expenditure.United's transfer activity has slowed since Belgium midfielder Youri Tielemans joined them for £35m on 14 July.While uncertainty over Rashford's future is not the entire reason for this, it is a basic truth that United's search for a left-sided attacking player, or another striker, will be affected if he stays at the club because he can play in both positions.Equally, the amount United can pay in wages will differ depending on whether Rashford's salary is part of the overall bill.Many fans are conflicted.Plenty feel Rashford's fallout with Amorim over his performances in training was reflective of someone who no longer felt the joy of playing for his boyhood club.Comparisons were made with his performances prior to his exit from United and those at Aston Villa, with England and then Barcelona.Others think Rashford is too good to be discarded; a local lad who would benefit from an arm around the shoulder and is capable of making a significant impact in Carrick's team.The secondary point to that is could United sign a player of similar standing for £26m, given that is the fee sources close to Rashford feel would not be exceeded given it had been agreed with Barcelona?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Marcus Rashford and Michael Carrick were Manchester United team-mates for three seasons up to 2018Rashford is 15th in United's all-time goalscorers chart with 138. He needs 17 more to equal Paul Scholes in 10th spot.Thirty-two of those goals were scored with Carrick as a team-mate.Carrick also coached Rashford, then managed him for three games in a 10-day spell in 2021 between Ole Gunnar Solskjaer getting sacked and Ralf Rangnick being brought in as the Norwegian's temporary replacement.The pair are said to get on well.Any return under Amorim would have been reminiscent of Jadon Sancho's peace deal with Erik ten Hag that got through one pre-season trip to the USA and a seven-minute Community Shield appearance against Manchester City before he moved to Chelsea on loan. But it is possible to see Carrick and Rashford working together with a degree of permanence.Carrick is yet to speak to the wider media since United returned to pre-season training.An expected partially open training session in Maynooth early next week has been scrapped, so, if Rashford does return as anticipated, there will be no external cameras to catch it.Clubs in the Premier League and overseas have inquired about Rashford and will surely continue to do so until the transfer window closes on 1 September.Manchester United continue to insist there will be no cut-price deal or loan.Unless something significant happens in the coming days, Rashford's return will be complete.Follow Manchester United on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical United contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about the Red Devils

schema.headline: Marcus Rashford: Will he return to Man Utd - and what impact would he have?

title: Farmers warn shoppers face smaller and more expensive vegetables due to hot weather
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Farmers said the dry weather could lead to higher prices or smaller vegetables for consumersByAlex DanielBusi
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Farmers said the dry weather could lead to higher prices or smaller vegetables for consumersByAlex DanielBusiness reporter and Esme StallardSenior climate and science reporterThis year's harvest could be the worst on record as farmers warn the exceptionally dry spring and summer could lead to "shrinkflation" in UK supermarkets.England and Wales saw their driest July since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, and a drought has been declared across large parts of the country.The Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank said the UK's cereals and oilseed harvest could be 2.5 million tonnes less than ​earlier forecasts.Tim O'Malley, the chairman of Nationwide produce, said it was "as bad as its ever been" and that shoppers will likely see higher prices or smaller vegetables in supermarkets.The harvest of barley, oats and rapeseed, which are used in beer, breakfast cereals and vegetable oil, is estimated to drop to just 19.5 million tonnes, the worst since records began in 1984.That is compared with a previous low of 19.8 million tonnes in 2020, and would cost farmers £390m in lost revenue, the ECIU estimated.The crops are also used for feeding livestock, making them crucial across most of the food chain.O'Malley said consumers could feel the impact in the vegetable aisle too, where grocers are likely to swap in smaller produce at the same price, which is known as shrinkflation."I think we're going to see shrinkflation," he told Radio 5 Live's Wake Up to Money."The problem we're going to have this year is a massive reduction in yield and major quality issues," O'Malley said.He said that will mean smaller sizes for fresh produce."We've got crop with stress or we've got quality issues. So you will see a smaller crop," O'Malley said.He said supermarkets will "do everything" to keep prices where they are, but added: "eventually they will probably have to come to the party and increase the price, particularly if they start importing."Grocers are already bringing in more products from abroad because of the poor conditions at home."We're importing broccoli and iceberg from Spain at this time of year, which in August [is] unheard of. I think we're going to see more of that, unfortunately," O'Malley said.He added: "Loud and clear, it's grim out there. I think it's as bad as it's ever been … Every record is being broken."The difference in this year and last year, last year we had four heat waves. But in between them we had a bit of rain."Farmers source additional water for their crops and livestock over summer from a combination of stored winter rainfall on site, and by extracting it from natural sources - a process called abstraction.This can be from groundwater or from surface water, like rivers and streams.This summer has seen significant low rainfall affecting the amount of water available to draw from.Half of England and all of Wales have been declared to be in drought conditions by the Environment Agency.Wales has received just 8% of its average rainfall so far this month. England has received 7% of its average, with that figure as low as 1% across southern England.The high temperatures and repeated heatwaves have also increased evaporation rates which have particularly hit rivers.Climate change is expected to bring more severe, frequent and longer-lasting heatwaves in UK summers in the coming years - which could bring more water shortages for farmers.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Experts said the the UK's cereals and oilseed harvest could be the worst since records began in 1984.Tom Lancaster, land, food and farming analyst at the ECIU said: "At the start of spring farmers were hopeful of a better year, but the dry April and July and record-breaking heat have left farmers facing down the barrel of a third awful harvest in a row."Farming is now the sector most exposed to climate change and the risks and damage that it brings."Martin Lines, head of the Nature Friendly Farming Network and a farmer from Cambridgeshire, said this year's harvest "has been a real kick in the teeth"."After two terrible harvests in a row, the crops this year were looking good and full of potential coming out of spring, only for months of drought and heatwaves to destroy any prospect of a decent harvest," he said."I've never known it this dry and hot on our farm."Even farmers I know who were sceptical of climate change are now saying they're really worried about the future of their businesses and production, it's just been completely brutal for our industry."Get in touchHas your farm or business been affected by the extreme weather?

schema.headline: Farmers warn shoppers face smaller and more expensive vegetables due to hot weather

title: The cost of being single – and how friends are teaming up to beat it
description: Image source, Leanne and Sarah/BBCImage caption, Sarah and Leanne say their decision to buy a house together as friends worked out wellByJemma CrewBus
body: Image source, Leanne and Sarah/BBCImage caption, Sarah and Leanne say their decision to buy a house together as friends worked out wellByJemma CrewBusiness reporter When Leanne split up with her partner in her late 20s she thought she'd have to put her dream of a buying a home in the area where she grew up on hold.She was earning a good salary but the properties she was hoping for - with a garden and parking space - were too expensive on her own. While she'd just started seeing someone new, it was very early days - far too early to discuss living together.Her friend since school, Sarah, was single and renting a room in a shared house in Brighton. She also wanted to move back home to Kent, but was worried about how she'd get on the housing ladder on her cabin crew salary.When Sarah suggested they buy together, Leanne admits she "totally baulked". But after chatting with a mortgage adviser they went ahead - and say it's helped them avoid the so-called singles tax.Not being partnered up can mean extra costs. It's tricky to quantify and varies by location - estimates suggest it could be anything from hundreds of pounds to £10,000 on average extra, external a year.The cost of rent or a mortgage, household bills and subscriptions can't be shared. And a single person pays 25% less council tax than a couple - not half.Many discounts involve pairing up - 2-for-1 cinema tickets, Two-Together railcards, couples gym memberships - plus solo travellers often pay a single person supplement.This affects a lot of people. Some 18.5m people had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2024 – 36.8% of the population aged 16 and over, official figures show.And overall 8.6m people were estimated to be living alone in the UK last year - that's nearly a third of all households.Ahead of their house purchase, Sarah and Leanne agreed a minimum amount of time they'd live together for - two years, which they then extended to four - and discussed what would happen if one person wanted to leave. Their mortgage payments were split proportionally to take into account their differing salaries, and the arrangements detailed in a declaration of trust so they would be protected when they came to sell. They were able to split the household bills - with these coming out of a joint account and self-professed "bill keeper" Sarah keeping track of what they needed to transfer each month - but also cut costs by sharing some meals and the cooking as they had similar eating habits."We called it our happy home, not our forever home," says Leanne."And it was a very happy home," agrees Sarah. Image source, Leanne and Sarah/BBCImage caption, Leanne and Sarah call the place they bought together their "happy home"Benefits to buying a home with friends include a bigger deposit and budget, and split costs, according to the Homeowner's Alliance. But it says people should consider potential pitfalls seriously and plan ahead by being upfront about their finances, seeking separate legal advice and drawing up a formal agreement.Sarah and Leanne sold their house for a profit four years after moving in, and they put the equity they'd built up toward their next, separate purchases."Neither of us would have been able to do what we've done without having the property that we had together," says Sarah. "It's brought us a lot of freedom."Leanne thinks she would have been able to afford what she wanted in time, but the financial benefits from buying with Sarah made this possible much sooner."The hidden singles tax is that everything has to take so much longer for you to be able to be in a position of affordability to do what you want to do," she adds.Their success inspired their friend Philly to set up Cucoon - an online platform matching up singles to potentially buy together.She says her aim is to "level the playing field", adding the singles tax is particularly high when it comes to housing.How to cut costs if you're singleMonetise your real estate: rent out rooms, car parking spaces and garagesShared dinners: hosts take turns to cook with larger, cheaper productsBorrowing circles: one person buys an expensive item, such as a lawnmower, and passes it alongErrand pooling: friends share fuel costs by taking it in turns to drive to the supermarketJulia Pearson, from Hampshire, set up the Just4One website about nine years ago when she wanted to go on holiday and discovered many places would charge her extra if she went alone.Alongside practical support for solo life, the platform lists travel providers which do not include the single supplement.Being single feels like a "constant review of your costs all the time", she says.In a list of a money-saving tips for drivers, the RAC suggests adding a named driver onto your car insurance., externalIt's something Julia has tried - and says it's saved her 8%.The RAC says this can bring your premium down, but warns it can also do the opposite.Julia also shares items with friends – she has borrowed tools to renovate her home and given people plant cuttings from her garden."I think as a society, we are becoming more social in terms of our sharing and thinking."Rather than thinking, 'I've got to go out and buy that', think about how else can you play that, what else can you do aside from having to buy something?"And it's good for the social side as well, two benefits in one."Get in touchHow have you managed to cut costs in different areas of your life? Share your tipsGet our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: The cost of being single – and how friends are teaming up to beat it

title: FGM: 'My grandmother subjected my baby to female genital mutilation behind my back'
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, It is believed FGM is more prevalent in the Emberá community than official statistics suggestByJosé C
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, It is believed FGM is more prevalent in the Emberá community than official statistics suggestByJosé Carlos CuetoBBC News Mundo reporting from ColombiaWarning: This story contains descriptions of the practices involved in female genital mutilationIn what activists are calling a milestone, Colombia last week became the first country in Latin America where female genital mutilation (FGM) is now illegal.As José Carlos Cueto reports, while the bill was passed unanimously in Colombia's Congress, it follows a long battle to eradicate the dangerous and often secretive procedure.Carla Quiñonez's daughter was just six months old when the baby's great-grandmother subjected her to female genital mutilation (FGM).Quiñonez (not her real name) says when her grandmother returned the baby to her, she had a fever and was swollen and bleeding. She cried constantly. "I confronted my grandmother, but she said it was normal and that I could not tell anyone."The nearest health centre was a long journey away, so Quiñonez's mother, a midwife, tried to ease the baby's pain with medicinal plants. She also challenged Quiñonez's grandmother. But the older woman would not listen. "She said that men make fun of women who have a clitoris."FGM in ColombiaImage caption, Carla Quiñonez is an activist working to end female genital cutting within her Emberá communityFGM involves the partial or total removal of the external female genitalia, as well as other injuries inflicted on those organs for non-medical reasons. It can cause medical complications, including haemorrhaging and infection, as well as complications later in life with periods and during childbirth. It can also make it difficult for a woman to experience sexual pleasure.The World Health Organization says that around the world more than 230 million girls and women alive today have been cut, predominantly in Africa.Quiñonez, 30, has been campaigning to eradicate the practice in Colombia - where it is still practised by members of her Emberá Indigenous community.  Along with fellow activists and members of Colombia's Congress, she played a key role in the campaign which led to the ban.She says it was only as she grew up that she realised what was secretly happening within her community."I always wondered why more girls than boys seemed to die shortly after birth."I remember a young cousin of mine whose birth was attended by my mother. She was born healthy, but died three days later."I asked my mother about it, and she told me the baby had died from 'jai', an ancestral illness."Quiñonez now believes that girls who supposedly died from "jai" actually died from complications related to FGM.A paediatrician's perspectiveImage source, Courtesy of Diana Ramos / Photo by David JiménezImage caption, Paediatrician Diana Ramos wants doctors to be better educated about FGMBetween 2020 and June 2026, 240 cases of FGM were recorded in Colombia. In the vast majority of instances, the girls were younger than six years old. But paediatrician Diana Ramos Mosquera says she believes this is just "the tip of the iceberg".Working at San Jorge University Hospital in Pereira, a city in Colombia's north-west coffee-growing region, she says she's seen signs of scarring, burning and mutilation when examining girls who have come in with other medical conditions.She recalls one girl who arrived with her vaginal opening sealed shut, meaning she probably would not have been able to menstruate or have sexual intercourse when she reached adulthood."She had to undergo reconstructive surgery," Dr Ramos says. She regards FGM as a form of sexual and gender-based violence with lifelong consequences, but says this must be addressed through education, and not just punishment."Some members of these communities genuinely believe they are doing no harm," she says.'Culture does not kill'Image source, José Carlos Cueto / BBC MundoImage caption, Juliana Domico, the legal representative of the Emberá Confederation, pushed for the bill's passageWith around 300,000 members, the Great Emberá Nation is one of Colombia's largest Indigenous communities, with populations also living in Ecuador and Panama.One theory about why members of the community practise FGM, when it's rarely seen elsewhere in Latin America, is that the practice arrived with enslaved people from African countries. This could help explain its prevalence in Risaralda, Chocó and Valle del Cauca, neighbouring departments that either are home to, or border, large Afro-Colombian populations.Another theory is that the birth of an intersex child, hundreds of years ago, left the community with a fear of the clitoris - with many older women believing that it will grow into a penis if not cut.Others think that it stems from the patriarchal belief that a woman with an organ associated with sexual pleasure is more likely to be promiscuous.Whatever its origin, Juliana Domico, the legal representative and chief Indigenous councillor to the National Confederation of the Peoples of the Great Emberá Nation of Colombia, rejects the idea that the practice is cultural."Our culture is our clothing, our crafts, our dances and our language, not a practice that kills. Culture does not kill."She says the new law follows years of advocacy work within the community: "We hope the law is translated into public policy, with sufficient resources to implement it."Threats and hostilityImage caption, Quiñonez says while FGM is considered a 'woman's issue', male authority figures have created obstacles to changeQuiñonez is one of those who have advocated for change, but says she has received threats because of this - especially from men. While, traditionally, men are not meant to know about the ritual, conversations about abolishing the practice often only take place with male leaders because many Emberá women speak an indigenous language - also called Emberá - and have not necessarily learned Spanish. This can also prevent women from accessing help from doctors for their babies, a problem which Quiñonez says is compounded when they're faced by sometimes ill-informed and judgmental health staff.She says when she took her daughter to hospital with a fever caused by a urinary tract infection, the nurse berated her for "being a savage" and told her that she had got what she deserved."I was even threatened with having my daughter taken away and placed in the care of the child welfare authorities."Since then, I prefer not to take my daughter to hospital. I treat her with medicinal plants and medication. I never leave her side."'Conversation cannot be avoided'Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Activists hope the new law will also bring with it more education about the damage FGM causes Quiñonez says that there is change under way within the Emberá community, with women now discussing among themselves whether FGM should happen. She says she was moved when one grandmother reflected on carrying out FGM on her granddaughters. "She said she had never acted out of malice and had only wanted to prevent men from criticising her granddaughters."Having conversations about a different way of life can be painful, she says. "Women who have grown up without a clitoris cannot imagine a different body." It will also be difficult to speak to her own daughter about it, one day in the future, "but it is a conversation that cannot be avoided," she says. "All of us deserve to understand our bodies and to talk about them without shame."Illustrations by Daniel Arce, from BBC Mundo's Visual Journalism Team.If you've been affected by issues raised in this story, sources of support are available via the BBC Action Line

schema.headline: FGM: 'My grandmother subjected my baby to female genital mutilation behind my back'

title: Gianni Infantino latest: Key questions as Fifa president faces executives
description: BBC Sport understands the meeting will take place at Fifa's Africa office in Rabat.It will include Grafstrom and members of the Fifa management board.
body: BBC Sport understands the meeting will take place at Fifa's Africa office in Rabat.It will include Grafstrom and members of the Fifa management board.Among those in attendance will be finance chief Thomas Peyer, legal chief Emilio Garcia Silvero, chief of staff Daniel O'Toole, chief of member associations Elkhan Mammadov and media relations director Bryan Swanson.It is unclear the intention of the meeting, but it is expected that Infantino will attempt to build bridges in an attempt to create a path to remaining as president.However, this may not be straightforward.In his letter to Fifa staff, Grafstrom said the events of the past week had been "a sad and reproachable series of events" which were "difficult to comprehend and accept".On Friday, Kevin Lamour, Fifa's chief operating officer, said the private investment plan was "the project of one person". He added Fifa's own administration was "deceived".Infantino will have to show contrition and perhaps offer a route to reform if he is to win back the support of his inner circle.Carlos Cordeiro, Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance, quit on Friday over the plan.Cordeiro said the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".Member associations had been given a deadline of 19 September to approve the plan or miss out on the extra funding that came as part of the deal. In his resignation announcement, Cordeiro offered a series of questions which Infantino will likely face at Wednesday's meeting. "Most troubling of all," Mr Cordeiro said, "is the absence of answers to fundamental questions. "Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?"These questions remain largely unanswered, and yet member associations are being asked to make a decision of enormous consequence in barely 50 days or risk being left behind."That is not a responsible way to determine the future of the world's game."This proposal has become a defining question for Fifa's future."On top of this, Infantino may also have to map out - or could offer - a route for reform. This may involve putting additional checks and balances in place that would make it impossible for such a plan to be devised and presented in this way again.Perhaps he could shelve his plans for a 64-team World Cup? Or offer to open up Fifa's cash reserves?It seems unlikely that Infantino will leave his position as Fifa president by the end of Wednesday.Infantino has, so far, shown no indication he is considering relinquishing his position. Indeed, he has been trying to rally his core supporter base around the globe.On Tuesday we saw African countries Egypt, Morocco, Niger, Mauritania and DR Congo all issue statements in support of Infantino. Infantino will, however, have to answer serious questions about a hugely controversial and damaging week for Fifa. There may be those in the room who will query his ability to turn this around, especially with such fierce criticism from European countries.Could that criticism be strong enough for Infantino to tender his resignation?More likely, perhaps, Infantino could see this as the start of the fightback.We may see a statement that will include an apology and a promise of change.If Infantino does vow to fight on, Uefa and countries from other confederations must look to find other ways to oust him.What other avenues are open?The Fifa Council could try to force Infantino's hand through an emergency meeting.Such a gathering would be triggered if 19 of the 37 Fifa Council members call for one.However, BBC Sport understands there are doubts that the 19 votes could be achieved.Another step could be an extraordinary congress of the 211 Fifa member associations, which would be held if one-fifth, or 43 associations, "make such a request in writing".So Uefa, which has 55 nations, can trigger the extraordinary congress whenever it wishes.That would take a minimum of two months from the point it is triggered, but more likely three months, and there is no guarantee of success.In effect, it would be a de facto election without there being another candidate as 106 votes would be needed to pass the vote of no confidence.Infantino would have time to win back votes from those who had been angered by the investment plan.Uefa can only really go down this route if it is confident of getting over the line.Which leaves finding a suitable candidate to fight the election at the Fifa Congress in March.Infantino stood unopposed when he was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 and if someone wants to battle him for the position, the deadline to announce their candidacy is 18 November.Concacaf president Victor Montagliani is seen as the most likely unity candidate to stand against Infantino.But there should be no expectation of success. Even at the height of the Fifa scandal in 2015, Sepp Blatter was re-elected as president eight days before he eventually resigned. If Infantino is still in position later on Wednesday, this story could yet have a long way to run.Inside Fifa, the expectation is that Infantino has called the meeting in Rabat in an attempt to clear the air, have a show of unity and try to achieve some alignment with his senior staff.But while that may be the beleaguered president's intention, what remains uncertain is what kind of response he will receive from those present, especially given the highly critical statements issued in recent days by chief of global football development Wenger, secretary general Grafstrom and chief operating officer Lamour.Some staff are asking if that could have emboldened others at the top of the organisation to speak out against him or to even insist he steps down.It is no surprise Infantino has chosen Morocco, where he has been based over the past week. Morocco is friendly territory for him. Not only is the country hosting the next World Cup, its national football association has come out in support of him. And it is where he still hopes to be re-elected for a fourth term at next year's Congress.The Uefa-led rebellion against him will be hoping that it does not get that far, and that he has been forced to quit long before then.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino latest: Key questions as Fifa president faces executives

title: The Mummy film ad banned from London Underground
description: Posters for the new The Mummy film have been banned from the London Underground and other billboards after regulators said they included realistic dep
body: Posters for the new The Mummy film have been banned from the London Underground and other billboards after regulators said they included realistic depictions of a dead child.The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) received 30 complaints regarding the promotional campaign for the Lee Cronin film and said the posters must not be displayed in areas where children could see them.Many complainants argued the imagery was distressing for both children and adults.Warner Bros defended the campaign, stating it had been prepared with "due responsibility to consumers and society" and was not designed to create fear or offence.The poster shows a close-up image of a female figure with a mummified appearance, sunken features and one eye swollen shut, alongside the tagline: "Some things are meant to stay buried."The distributor explained that the character depicted was a "living mummy" who was returned to her parents as a young adult, many years after having been kidnapped as a child. It argued that the poster used a neutral facial expression while avoiding elements of violence or intimidation to reduce any risk of distress. Warner Bros added that the design had been cleared by Transport for London's advertising partner, Global, for display across the London Underground network.However, the ASA upheld the complaints regarding the outdoor and Underground posters.The watchdog noted that the figure's grey, ashen skin, cracked lips and fixed, vacant expression combined to give a "realistic impression of a dead child".The ASA stated: "Because the figure had recognisable human features, we considered that viewers were likely to understand it as a realistic depiction of a dead child."

schema.headline: The Mummy film ad banned from London Underground
